Independent analysis of Census 2022

Health and Deprivation Across Ireland's Communities

Mankirat Singh · Portfolio · GitHub · LinkedIn

Independent analysis of CSO Census 2022 Small Area Population Statistics for all 3,420 Electoral Divisions. Not an official CSO publication. All findings describe areas, not individuals, and are associations, not proof of cause.

Key findings

  • In Census 2022, 1.9% of people reported bad or very bad health. Across the 3,420 Electoral Divisions this ranged from 0.7% to 2.9% (10th to 90th percentile).
  • Age structure alone explains 1% of the variation between communities (tested on counties the model never saw). Adding jobs, education and housing raises this to 63%.
  • After allowing for age, the strongest link is with primary education or less: a one-standard-deviation higher share goes with 0.28 pp more bad health (95% CI 0.25 to 0.32).
  • Communities fall into 3 profiles. Bad health is 2.8% in "Lower education & High unemployment" areas against 1.5% in "Highly educated & Private renters" areas.
  • 55 communities of 1,000+ people have bad-health rates at least 2 pp above what their age profile predicts: a practical shortlist for closer local attention.

2. Where bad health is concentrated

County rates are not age-adjusted: areas with older populations will show more bad health for that reason alone. Section 6 separates the two.

3. What bad health is linked to

Simple correlations across Electoral Divisions (weighted by population):

Degree or higher (%)-0.47

Many of these factors move together, so a regression estimates each one while holding the others fixed. Effects are per one standard deviation (SD), so they can be compared directly. The largest variance inflation factor is 3.0: the predictors are distinct enough to separate.

4. How well can we predict it?

To check the patterns are real and not just fitted noise, each model was trained on most counties and tested on counties it had never seen (5-fold cross-validation by county, so neighbouring areas cannot leak into the test). A random forest was included to catch non-linear patterns.

The random forest adds little over the linear model, so the simpler, explainable model is preferred. Its most important inputs were unemployment rate, primary education or less, households in social housing.

5. Community profiles

Grouping Electoral Divisions by age, jobs, education and housing (k-means, k = 3 chosen by silhouette score) gives distinct types of community. Health was not used to form the groups, so the differences below are a genuine test.

7. What this could mean for policy

  • Health need is local: rates differ several-fold between nearby communities, so county averages hide where need is greatest.
  • Age explains part of the picture, but jobs, education and housing explain substantially more, pointing to joined-up responses across health, employment, education and housing.
  • The community profiles and the "above expected" shortlist give a transparent, reproducible starting point for targeting, to be combined with local knowledge and health-service data.

Limitations and methods

  • Ecological fallacy: results describe areas. They do not show that unemployed or less-educated individuals are themselves in worse health.
  • Association, not cause: poor health can also lead to unemployment and lower income, so effects run both ways. "Unable to work due to illness or disability" was deliberately not used as a predictor, because it partly measures the outcome.
  • Self-reported health on Census night (April 2022); people who did not state their health are excluded from rates.
  • Methods: population-weighted least squares with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) 95% intervals; variance inflation factors; random forest with county-grouped cross-validation and permutation importance; k-means on standardised indicators. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib). Predictors: Aged 65 and over, Unemployment rate, Primary education or less, Households in social housing, Households renting privately.
  • Data: CSO Census 2022 SAPS tables SAP2022T12T3ED, SAP2022T1T1AED, SAP2022T10T4ED, SAP2022T8T1ED and SAP2022T6T3ED via the CSO PxStat API; ED boundaries from Tailte Éireann / CSO (generalised 50m). Code: GitHub.
